newsitem.title: USA: Clinton, Yeltsin to meet in Helsinki March 20-21.
newsitem.headline: Clinton, Yeltsin to meet in Helsinki March 20-21.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton and Russian President Boris Yeltsin will hold their next summit on March 20-21 in Helsinki, Finland, convenient to the ailing Russian's Moscow home base, it was announced on Friday.

Confirming that the site had been shifted from the United States, which was due to host the meeting, U.S. Vice President Al Gore and Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin announced agreement on the date and place and said the summit would address important security and economic issues.

"This will of course be an important meeting and we expect among other things that the presidents will address bilateral arms control, European security and a number of economic issues of importance to our peoples," Gore said at a news conference with Chernomyrdin after two days of talks.
Chernomyrdin later met Clinton in the Oval Office, and the president said at an opening, picture-taking session he was "looking forward" to the summit with Yeltsin.
"It will be very important and I feel quite optimistic about it because of the good relationshipship I've always had with President Yeltsin," Clinton said.
He said he hoped the talks would ease Russian concerns about the expansion of NATO and "make it clear that no one has any intention of providing any increased threat to Russia."

"I believe that we ought to work out an agreement between NATO and Russia and involving the United States which ensures that Russia will have a leading role in European security affairs," Clinton said.
NATO is expected to announce this summer it is inviting Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic, all former Soviet allies, to join its ranks.

Chernomyrdin has voiced anxiety that such a move would undermine Yeltsin's government and give impetus to ultranationalists in Russia. Earlier on Friday, Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov said in Moscow that failure to address these concerns could bring about "serious changes" in Russian foreign policy.
Gore and Chernomyrdin have met every six months for the last four years at the head of a Cabinet-level U.S.-Russian liaison group originally assigned to discuss nuts-and-bolts issues of technology.

More recently, however, it has become the key channel of diplomatic communication between Moscow and Washington, especially since health problems left Yeltsin more and more often indisposed since last year.

It was Yeltsin's turn to visit the United States, since Clinton went to Moscow for the last summit in April. But in deference to the Russian president's ongoing recuperation from heart surgery and pneumonia, U.S. officials agreed to move the meeting to a site closer to Russia.

Clinton said Helsinki "works well for both of us," and told reporters he was eager to visit the Finnish capital. It is just across the Russo-Finnish border, a relatively short plane ride or an overnight train journey from Moscow.

Asked about Yeltsin's health at a news conference and signing ceremony, Chernomyrdin replied: "The president is not able to be constantly in the office now. He's not in good enough health for this...."
But Chernomyrdin added, "The president is recovering and he oversees all the necessary issues."
Yeltsin cancelled a visit to the Netherlands earlier this month and is under doctors' orders to limit his workload.

He was shown on television on Thursday addressing the nation directly for the first time since his release from the hospital on Jan. 20 after treatment for pneumonia. He spoke for less than a minute on a pension controversy.
His voice was steady, his speech slow and his manner determined, but he had clearly aged considerably since a quintuple heart bypass operation in November.
Gore and Chernomyrdin signed 22 agreements during the course of their two-day meeting, most aimed at fostering foreign investment in Russia.

They also announced agreements worth $355 million signed by the Overseas Private Investment Corporation for five U.S. projects in Russia, including $116 million for the first oil project since Russia passed new oil and gas legislation.
